statement.text:
2. Chimney physics
A furnace at temperature \(T_\mathrm{Smoke}\) produces volume \(B\) of gas per unit time. A chimney of cross-section \(A\) and height \(h\) releases it into ambient air at \(T_\mathrm{Air}\). Take \(g=9.81\,\mathrm{m/s^2}\).
Assume negligible gas velocity in the furnace. Smoke and air have equal densities at equal temperature and pressure, and the furnace gas is ideal. Atmospheric pressure follows the hydrostatic law, with negligible air-density change over the chimney height. Smoke density is also constant along the chimney. Bernoulli's law applies:
\[\frac12\rho v(z)^2+\rho gz+p(z)=\mathrm{const}.\]

1.a
Find the minimum chimney height that releases all produced gas. Express it in \(B,A,T_\mathrm{Air},g\) and \(\Delta T=T_\mathrm{Smoke}-T_\mathrm{Air}\). Use this minimum height throughout the remaining tasks.
1.b
Two otherwise identical chimneys serve a \(400^\circ\mathrm C\) furnace. The one designed for ambient \(-30^\circ\mathrm C\) is \(100\,\mathrm m\) high. Find the height needed at \(+30^\circ\mathrm C\).
1.c
Sketch gas velocity versus height for a constant-area chimney. Mark the gas entry point.
1.d
Describe how smoke pressure varies with height.
Solar power plant
Sunlight heats air beneath an open-edged collector of area \(S\). Hot air rises through a chimney and draws in cold air. A turbine can extract kinetic energy from the flow. The incoming solar power per horizontal area is \(G\), all used to heat the air, with constant specific heat \(c\). Define efficiency as the ratio of gas-flow kinetic energy to the solar heat supplied before chimney entry.

2.a
Find this solar-chimney efficiency.
2.b
Sketch efficiency as a function of chimney height.
The Manzanares prototype has height \(195\,\mathrm m\), chimney radius \(5\,\mathrm m\), and circular collector diameter \(244\,\mathrm m\). Use \(c=1012\,\mathrm{J/(kg\,K)}\), hot-air density \(\rho_h=0.9\,\mathrm{kg/m^3}\), ambient temperature \(295\,\mathrm K\) and solar power \(G=150\,\mathrm{W/m^2}\).
3.a
Evaluate the prototype's efficiency.
3.b
Find the power it could produce.
3.c
Estimate its energy production during a typical sunny day.
4.a
Find the temperature rise as ambient air enters the chimney, both as a general formula and numerically for the prototype.
4.b
Find the air mass flow rate.

solution.text:
2. Chimney physics
1.a. Draft and minimum height
Let \(p_0\) be ambient pressure at the furnace level. Hydrostatics gives \(p_\mathrm{Air}(z)=p_0-\rho_a gz\). At minimum height smoke exit pressure equals the outside pressure. Bernoulli between the nearly stationary furnace gas and the exit gives
\[\frac12\rho_s v^2+\rho_sgh+p_0-\rho_agh=p_0,\qquad v^2=2gh\left(\frac{\rho_a}{\rho_s}-1\right).\]
Equal-pressure ideal-gas densities satisfy \(\rho_a/\rho_s=T_\mathrm{Smoke}/T_\mathrm{Air}\). To carry the produced gas, \(v\ge B/A\). Thus
\[h_{\min}=\frac{B^2T_\mathrm{Air}}{2gA^2\Delta T}.\]
1.b. Different climates
Absolute temperatures must be in kelvin. Keeping \(B,A\) and furnace temperature fixed, \(h\propto T_\mathrm{Air}/(T_\mathrm{Smoke}-T_\mathrm{Air})\). Hence
\[h_\mathrm{warm}=100\,\mathrm m\frac{303.15/(673.15-303.15)}{243.15/(673.15-243.15)}\simeq145\,\mathrm m.\]
1.c and 1.d. Flow and pressure profiles
Continuity with fixed density and cross-section makes \(v=B/A\) constant throughout the chimney. In the idealized model it jumps from nearly zero in the furnace to this value at entry. Smoke pressure drops at entry by \(\rho_s v^2/2=(\rho_a-\rho_s)gh\), then falls linearly:
\[p_\mathrm{Smoke}(z)=p_0-(\rho_a-\rho_s)gh-\rho_sgz,\qquad0<z<h.\]
At the top it matches ambient pressure. Draw the entry discontinuity and the different slopes rather than a continuously accelerating constant-area flow.
2. Solar-chimney efficiency
Write mass flow as \(\dot M=A\rho_h v\). The solar heating power is \(GS=\dot M c\Delta T\), while kinetic power is \(\dot Mv^2/2=\dot Mgh\Delta T/T_\mathrm{Air}\). Their ratio is
\[\eta=\frac{gh}{cT_\mathrm{Air}}.\]
The graph is a straight line through the origin with slope g/(c T_Air), within the assumptions of the chimney model. It should not be extrapolated to efficiencies above one.
3. Prototype numbers
\[\eta=\frac{9.81\times195}{1012\times295}\simeq0.0064=0.64\%,\qquad P=GS\eta\simeq45\,\mathrm{kW}.\]
A typical sunny-day duration is not specified in the statement. The official estimate assumes eight hours, giving \(E\simeq360\,\mathrm{kWh}\). For any chosen duration \(t_d\), use \(E=GS\eta t_d\). The numeric field states the eight-hour convention.
4. Temperature rise and mass flow
Eliminate mass flow between \(\dot M=A\rho_h\sqrt{2gh\Delta T/T_\mathrm{Air}}\) and \(\dot M=GS/(c\Delta T)\). This gives
\[\Delta T=\left[\frac{G^2S^2T_\mathrm{Air}}{2ghA^2c^2\rho_h^2}\right]^{1/3}\simeq9.1\,\mathrm K,\qquad \dot M=\frac{GS}{c\Delta T}\simeq760\,\mathrm{kg/s}.\]
These are ideal available kinetic-energy figures, not an additional claim about actual electrical output or turbine efficiency. The original solution cites W. W. Christie's Chimney design and theory (1902), and Schlaich, Bergermann, Schiel and Weinrebe, Design of Commercial Solar Updraft Tower Systems (2005). Its original references and equations remain in the linked PDF.
